I spoke to you previously about a number of things.
I asked you about my initial work on implementing a custom Jinja2 `ChoiceLoader` and template cache within `flask/templating.py` and `flask/blueprints.py`, which we verified using `tests/test_blueprints.py` and `tests/test_templating.py`. We also addressed a regression in `tests/test_basic.py` by utilizing `has_request_context()` in `flask/templating.py`, while updating `docs/changes.rst` and the `Blueprint` class docstring in `flask/blueprints.py`.

Following a maintainer's concern regarding potential performance overhead from `jinja2.ChoiceLoader`, you suggested I investigate `flask/app.py` and consider using `functools.lru_cache` in `flask/templating.py` to memoize blueprint template path resolution. I decided to keep this logic within `flask/templating.py` to maintain encapsulation, ensuring I used the blueprint's object ID as a cache key to prevent stale lookups.

After implementing the cache, I observed a 15 percent performance improvement in `render_template` execution. I added a stress test to `tests/test_templates.py` to verify stability under load and updated my existing pull request with these optimizations. Following your advice, I monitored the CI logs, and after confirming that all tests in `tests/test_templates.py` passed across multiple Python versions, I received approval from the maintainer.
It has been quite a journey. From my initial confusion in 'test.py' to now fixing core template resolution logic. I really appreciate your patience and guidance throughout this entire process.
It has been my pleasure. You tackled a complex issue, navigated the codebase successfully, and handled performance considerations like a pro. This is exactly what open-source collaboration is about.
Should I close out the issue tracker manually once it's merged, or do the maintainers usually take care of that? I want to make sure I follow proper protocol.
Usually, referencing the issue number in your commit messages or the PR body will cause GitHub to automatically close the issue upon merging. You don't need to do anything else. Enjoy your success!
Thanks again for the guidance. I noticed a small typo in my final commit message for the 'render_template' fix. Does that matter for the project history, or should I leave it?
Don't worry too much about it. As long as the commit references the correct issue #1361, the maintainers care more about the functional integrity of 'flask/templating.py' than a typo in the log.
That makes sense. I was worried it might look unprofessional, but I suppose the codebase cleanliness in 'tests/test_templates.py' is the real priority.
Exactly. The code review process in 'pallets/flask' is rigorous precisely because they value the long-term maintainability of the project. A typo in a commit log is inconsequential.
I'm starting to look at other issues now. Is it standard practice to write a reproduction script like I did with 'test.py' before diving into the core logic?
Yes, absolutely. Building a standalone reproduction script or a minimal test case is the gold standard for submitting a patch to 'Flask'. It prevents regressions.
Do you think the 'lru_cache' I added to the lookup mechanism might have any negative side effects if the 'template_folder' path changes dynamically at runtime?
That's a valid concern. In 'flask', blueprints are usually initialized at startup. If you anticipate dynamic folder swapping, you might need to use 'cache_clear()' when that property is modified.
Good point. I'll add a note in the docs or a comment in 'flask/blueprints.py' explaining that the cache assumes a static configuration for template paths.
Adding an inline comment is a great practice. It signals to future maintainers that you considered the edge case, even if you decided not to support dynamic updates right now.
What about testing that caching behavior? Should I add another test case to 'tests/test_templates.py' that specifically triggers a cache miss?
Yes, testing the cache hit/miss ratio can be done with 'unittest.mock' to count calls. It provides certainty that your optimization is actually working as intended.
I will include that as a follow-up PR if the current one is merged. I don't want to overcomplicate the scope of the fix for #1361 right now.
Wise move. Staying focused on the original issue scope is the best way to ensure your primary PR gets merged quickly without unnecessary churn.
Should I add a 'CHANGES.rst' entry for this fix, or is that something the maintainers prefer to handle themselves during the release cycle?
Usually, the maintainers appreciate you adding a line to 'CHANGES.rst' under the 'Improvements' or 'Bug Fixes' section. It shows you respect the release process.
I'll submit one final update to the PR with the 'CHANGES.rst' entry. Thanks for helping me navigate this, it feels like I've learned the 'Flask' internal workflow.
You certainly have. You’ve successfully navigated everything from local reproduction in 'start.py' to performance tuning and documentation. That is the complete cycle.
I'm ready to move on to my next task now. It's been a great learning experience. Thanks for your help!
Ok.
You're very welcome! I'm glad I could assist. Good luck with your next issue, and feel free to reach out if you hit another wall in the 'Flask' codebase.
